source_refs.note: Topic 24.6 (PDF 129-130); the structures are redrawn. The book's zwitterion is printed without charges ('R-C-COO', 'Nh3'). The essential amino acid count is given as the book states, with a note that most lists give nine for adults.

blocks.text: Amino acids are an important group of compounds that contain both a basic amino group (-NH2) and an acidic carboxylic acid group (-COOH). They are therefore amphoteric: they can behave as both acids and bases. The general structure of the alpha-amino acids (2-aminocarboxylic acids) is H2N-CH(R)-COOH.

An alpha-amino acid exists as a dipolar ion called a zwitterion, with a positive and a negative end in the same molecule. In forming the zwitterion a proton passes from the carboxyl group to the amino group: H3N+-CH(R)-COO-. The dipolar structure is also called an internal salt.

The R group is the part that varies between amino acids. The simplest amino acid is glycine (aminoethanoic acid), in which R is a hydrogen atom; in alanine (2-aminopropanoic acid) R is a methyl group, -CH3. Except glycine, all alpha-amino acids are chiral. Of the 20 alpha-amino acids, 10 are essential (the body cannot make them) and 10 are non-essential.

blocks.alt: Top: H2N-CH(R)-COOH, an alpha-amino acid, with an arrow showing H+ moving to give the zwitterion H3N+-CH(R)-COO-; glycine has R = H and alanine R = CH3, and all except glycine are chiral. Bottom: the cationic form H3N+-CH(R)-COOH at low pH, the dipolar ion at pH = pI, and the anionic form H2N-CH(R)-COO- at high pH, linked by OH- and H+ arrows along a pH axis.
blocks.caption: Amino acids, zwitterions and the forms present at different pH (original diagram after the book's structures).
blocks.long_description: An amino acid carries its own acid and base. The -COOH group gives a proton to the -NH2 group of the same molecule, giving the zwitterion. Adding acid puts a proton back on the carboxylate (cationic form); adding alkali removes the proton from -NH3+ (anionic form).
